items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: Lou McGarity was playing lead trombone, Panama Francis was in the rhythm section

ctx.x: That’s so interesting, that I mean it was very astute of you to really have that time off and spend that time digging ditches and really thinking about, now what am I going to do now, and really think about what people wanted to hear and songs they fell in love with, so that you were bringing the business and the music together. Where too often sometimes the businessmen don’t really know music at all. And you pulled them right together.

Yeah, they knew what I was doing too, and they liked the idea too of what I was doing. As a matter of fact I went to a place, a company called Institute of Motivational Research. They got very much interested in the project, and without charging me, they did some research on my product, and then Columbia Records got them into it and we did it further. But you know what was fun about it though, was I didn’t go all the way down the line and do like, you know Guy Lombardo commercial style, or — I can’t think of any…
Let me play something for you here.

items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: he always got in touch with me, and I would go on tours with him

ctx.x: Well, he had an idea of using voices like horns, you see, using voices like horns. Like, he liked the high voices of women, and they were the trumpets, and the low voices was the men. And so he came in with this drum part, which if I had played it the way it was written, it would never have happened. So I made a rhythm of my own with the brushes, and I mean, the only thing it was, it was the same rhythm I would play with sticks on the cymbal, but instead I was playing it on a snare drum, and it worked.

And so, from then on, I did all of his sessions using this rhythm. And even when he got ready to move out to California, he wanted me to gowith him, but I didn't go, but then again, every drummer out there hated me because he wanted them to play the same as I did on the record, and he lost a lot of friends who were drummers out in California because of that. But whnever he got ready to make a tour of any kind, he always got in touch with me, and I would go on tours with him, so I was with him in 1974 in England,…
And, I also went the following year -- 1975, I went to Japan with him.
